title: How Kepler caught a wine seller's one-stick trick
description:
Linz, 1613: Johannes Kepler buys wine for his wedding, and the seller prices every barrel by one rod pushed from the top hole to the far edge of the lid. With a 1 metre rod, a thin barrel 50 cm wide holds about 340 litres, while one 82 cm wide holds about 605: the same price for very different wine. Treat the barrel as a cylinder and the rod as a diagonal (rod² = width² + (half the length)²), and the volume peaks when the length is √2 times the width. Kepler found Austrian barrels were built close to that shape, and near a maximum the volume barely changes (10% off the shape loses under 1%), so the rod was fair for them. He published the method in Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum (1615).

Numbers checked in code: exact cylinder volumes for a 1 m rod, a brute-force search for the best width, and 100,000 random barrels within 10% of the ideal shape (worst loss 0.72%). Sources: Wikipedia, Johannes Kepler; matematicasvisuales.com, 'Kepler: The volume of a wine barrel'.

beats.say: Same stick, same price, 44% less wine.
A longer stick should mean more wine. Not if the barrel is thin.
Linz, 1613. Kepler buys wine for his wedding. The seller prices each barrel by one rod, dipped to the far corner.
Kepler is furious. A long thin barrel and a short fat one can both read 1 metre.
So check it yourself. The rod is a diagonal: the width, and half the length.
50 centimetres wide: 340 litres. Go wider and the wine climbs. At 82, it peaks: 605. Wider still, it falls.
So every rod has one best barrel. But was anyone's barrel built like that?
The best one is 1.4 times as long as it is wide. Kepler found Austrian barrels were close.
And at the peak, the curve is flat. 10% off that shape loses under 1% of the wine. The rod was fair.
